rationale: The book's core identification derives directly and uniformly from its prior tree=nation equation (explicitly decoded by Daniel and applied to Assyria/Pharaoh/Egypt as cedars among the trees of Eden). A planted stand of such trees is therefore a grouping of nations; Ezek 31:9 and the surrounding riddle make that equation natural, and the same figure coheres with 'all the trees of the field' as all nations (Ezek 17). The paradise reading, while dominant for Genesis–Revelation bookends and for watered-garden blessing language, treats the trees of Eden merely as poetic superlatives and leaves the nation-decoding of Daniel and Ezekiel unexploited. For the supplied texts the book's chain therefore carries the identification with fewer unsupported steps. Secondary elaborations (Isaiah gardens as political alliances, eternal clean/unclean diet, sealing of trees) are coherent extensions but not indispensable to the core and remain open to residual dispute.
book_core_identification: A planted stand of trees — a grouping of nations.
book_secondary_elaborations: Isaiah's 'gardens' (1:29–30; 65:3; 66:17) are the nations Judah chose to trust and sacrifice among rather than literal pagan groves
Isa 66:17 'after one in the midst' (no 'tree' in the Hebrew) means following a single nation and adopting its unclean practices
The food-law boundary remains eternal and is the ground of final judgment
The command 'Hurt not … the trees' (Rev 7:3) protects nations before the four winds are loosed
The garden of God is simply the field of nation-trees
strongest_counter_interpretation: In mainstream Christian teaching the garden is primarily the paradise of Eden: the ordered place of God's presence, unbroken communion, abundance and the tree of life, lost through expulsion and restored in the new creation (Gen 2–3 → Rev 22), with secondary layers (temple, bride, watered fruitfulness, Gethsemane/new-Adam typology) remaining complementary rather than rival.
counter_core_identification: Paradise / Eden as the place of God's presence and unbroken communion between God and humanity, lost and eschatologically restored.
material_core_denial: That the primary symbolic referent of 'garden' is a grouping of nations rather than the archetypal paradise of divine presence.
counter_case: Genesis 2:8–15 plants a literal garden in Eden containing the tree of life, a river and Adam; God walks there (3:8) and expels the man (3:23–24).
Prophetic restoration language repeatedly equates renewed Zion or land with 'Eden, the garden of the LORD' (Isa 51:3; Ezek 36:35).
Revelation deliberately re-uses tree-of-life and river-of-life imagery inside 'the paradise of God' (Rev 2:7; 22:1–5), closing the canonical arc.
Song of Songs 4:12–16 and related texts read the enclosed garden as bridal intimacy or the Church/soul; Gethsemane and the garden tomb supply new-Adam typology.
These readings enjoy settled consensus across Christian tradition and require no intermediate symbol chain.
book_explanatory_advantages: Rests on Daniel's own decoding of the great tree as the king and his kingdom (Dan 4:20–22), not on later allegory.
Species of tree consistently names the nation (cedar = Assyria/Pharaoh, vine/fig/olive = Israel) across Hosea, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Romans 11.
Ezek 31:9 places the envious 'trees of Eden … in the garden of God' immediately before the equation 'This is Pharaoh and all his multitude' (31:18), making the garden a stand of nation-trees.
Ezek 17:24's 'all the trees of the field' are likewise all nations under divine pruning; the garden figure simply gathers that forest.
Re-reads Isaiah's garden indictments inside oracles that already concern the nations, without requiring translators to insert 'tree' at 66:17.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Accounts for the foundational narrative setting of Genesis 2–3 without remainder.
Supplies the explicit canonical book-ends (Eden lost → paradise restored) that the book never addresses.
Explains the positive prophetic similes of restoration as return to Edenic blessing (Isa 51:3; Ezek 36:35; 47).
Naturally accommodates the Song of Songs, Gethsemane and Johannine garden-tomb scenes that the book leaves untouched.
Matches the broad, settled consensus of Christian exegesis rather than a novel system-internal definition.
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 31:3–18 (Pharaoh/Assyria as cedar among the trees of Eden in the garden of God)
Ezekiel 17:22–24 (all the trees of the field = all nations)
Isaiah 1:29–30; 65:3; 66:17 (gardens in oracles that concern the nations)
unresolved_objections: How (or whether) the definition applies to the original Genesis 2 garden, which is a single place prepared for one man rather than a grouping of nations
Whether Song of Songs, Gethsemane or the garden tomb can be read as 'groupings of nations' without special pleading
The secondary claim that clean/unclean food laws remain the ground of final judgment (Isa 66:17) sits in tension with Acts 10–11 and remains under-argued
